passage:
Gopika, you asked why I go quiet when people say "tell him from me". Your Vijay Mama will tell you.
When I was nineteen, my parents lived in one house but spoke only through me. At breakfast my father would clear his throat and say, "Tell your mother the electricity bill is not paid by magic." I carried it across the kitchen. My mother would say, "Tell him some of us work without being thanked." I carried that back.
Soon each of them began saying, "You understand me better than your mother," or, "You're the only sensible one, not like your father." I felt chosen and trapped at once. Whichever message I softened, one of them called me a traitor.
One evening I set down the tea and said, "From today, whatever you want to say, say it to each other." My legs were shaking.
It didn't fix them. But it gave me back my own place in that house.

qa.q: What did Vijay's father tell him to pass on at breakfast?
qa.a: His father said, "Tell your mother the electricity bill is not paid by magic."

qa.q: How did young Vijay feel when each parent called him the sensible one?
qa.a: He felt chosen and trapped at once, flattered but afraid of being called a traitor by whichever parent he disappointed.

qa.q: What choice inside the story gave young Vijay back his place?
qa.a: Setting down the tea and telling his parents to say things to each other, even with his legs shaking, stepped him out of the middle.

qa.q: How might Vijay's mother have felt when he refused to carry messages?
qa.a: She may have felt surprised and perhaps a little ashamed to see her son caught between them, and pushed to speak to his father directly.

grounding: An uncle recalls being used at nineteen as a go-between for his parents' hurtful messages, feeling divided and unsafe, and finally refusing to carry them.

The wedding hall was so loud with the band that Usha had to lean close to hear Akash, and she wished she hadn't.
"Kriti would've worn something brighter," he said of his ex, eyes on the stage. "She always knew how to dress for these things."
It was the fourth Kriti comment that month. Kriti cooked better. Kriti never got tired at parties. Each time Usha laughed it off, and each time she checked her reflection twice afterwards.
Now, in the crush near the food counter, a woman in a green saree said, "Arre, Akash! Where's Kriti these days?" Akash grinned. "Ask Usha, she's always thinking about her."
Usha felt her face burn. She wasn't thinking about Kriti. She was worried about never being enough.
Outside, by the parked scooters, she called her friend Mehak. "Can you pick me up? I'll explain on the way."

qa.q: How many Kriti comments had Akash made that month?
qa.a: It was the fourth Kriti comment that month.

qa.q: What was Usha truly worried about?
qa.a: She was worried about never being enough, not about Kriti, which shows how the comparisons had worn her down.

qa.q: Why was calling Mehak a wise step for Usha?
qa.a: Stepping out of the loud hall and calling a friend gave Usha support and space to think, instead of laughing off one more comparison.

qa.q: How does Akash seem to see his Kriti comments?
qa.a: He treats them as casual remarks and even jokes about them in public, seeming not to notice or care how much they unsettle Usha.

grounding: A young woman repeatedly compared to Akash's ex feels anxious and never good enough, and steps out of a wedding to call a friend for support.
